desc:
Cut nums into contiguous chunks. Then sort every chunk on its own (ascending) and glue the chunks back together in their original order. Return the largest number of chunks for which the glued result is the whole array sorted in ascending order.

nums = [2, 1, 3, 4, 4]
result = 4     ([2, 1] [3] [4] [4])
nums = [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
result = 1

Values may repeat, which makes this harder than the permutation version of the puzzle.
hints: A cut between positions i and i + 1 is allowed in the final answer only if nothing on the left needs to move past the cut.

The cut is safe exactly when every value on the left is less than or equal to every value on the right: max(nums[0..i]) ≤ min(nums[i+1..]). Cuts are independent of one another, so count the safe ones.

Compute suffix minima, sweep with a running prefix maximum, count the indices i < n - 1 with prefMax ≤ sufMin[i + 1] and answer count + 1. (A monotonic stack that stores the maximum of each chunk gives the same result in one pass.)
editorial: Sorting chunks independently and concatenating gives the globally sorted array iff, at every boundary, the left side only contains values that are no larger than anything on the right. If some left value were larger than a right value, the sorted chunks would leave those two in the wrong order; conversely, if each boundary satisfies the condition, then the sorted concatenation is sorted.

The conditions at different boundaries are independent, so the maximum number of chunks is one plus the number of positions i (between i and i + 1) with max(nums[0..i]) ≤ min(nums[i+1..n-1]). Equality is allowed because equal values can sit on either side of a cut without breaking the order.

Prefix maxima and suffix minima are computed in O(n), so the total is O(n) time and O(n) space. The stack alternative keeps one maximum per chunk: for each element, pop every chunk whose maximum is greater than the element and merge them into one chunk that keeps the largest of the popped maxima.
